3AnswerWestwood · Feb 6, 2012 · 50:17
① The Gemara answers. That in truth, the case of the Braisa of the secret thief can be referring to a case of an armed robber.
② Regarding the question of being redundant, the Gemara answers that there are two types of open thief:
ⓐ An armed robber.
ⓑ An open thief.

④ Therefore, the Braisa had to mention both.
⑤ Therefore, the Braisa can be learned like either Rava or Abaye, and therefore, the issue remains Unresolved.

lessons.expl:
4QuestionWestwood · Feb 13, 2012 · 21:47
① Mother [?] Braisa to try to resolve the dispute between Abaye/Rava.
② The Braisa says:
Ⅰ The case:
A river flooded away someone's beams, wood or stones and deposited them in someone else's field.
Ⅱ The din:
The finder may keep them.
Ⅲ The reason:
The Braisa says that the reason why the finder may keep them is because their owner already realized his loss and already gave up hope on them.
③ The Gemara now says on this Braisa:
It says that the finder may keep them only because the owner was already aware of his loss and he gave up hope.
④ This implies that in a different situation where the owner did not yet realize his loss, the finder may not keep it.
⑤ This is in spite of the fact that the object has no intrinsic sign.
⑥ Since it has no sign, we know for sure that when the owner discovers his loss, he will surely give up hope.
⑦ And even so, the finder may keep it, only if the owner already realized his loss and already gave up hope.
⑧ From this we see that in order for the finder to keep it, he must have actual giving up hope, and not potential.
⑨ This is a proof for Abaye, and a question on Rava.

6QuestionWestwood · Feb 20, 2012 · 36:23
① Rava explained the Braisa to be speaking about where the owner was able to save his object later on.
② The owner already gave up hope.
③ The Gemara now challenges Rava's explanation by introducing the end of this same Braisa.
④ There it says: if the owner chased after the object that was floating away, then the finder may not keep it.
⑤ The Gemara says: if this Braisa can be explained like Rava, to be talking about where the owner can save the object later on, then why, in the end of the Braisa, does it say that the finder may not keep it only if the owner did an action such as chasing it to indicate that he does not give up hope.
⑥ If the Braisa is talking about where the owner can save his object later on, then even if the owner would do nothing at all, even so, the finder cannot keep it, since a non-action on the part of the owner does not indicate giving up hope, since the owner relies on saving it later.
⑦ Since the Braisa says the finder cannot keep it, only if the owner did an action like chasing it, which implies his non-action indicates his giving up hope, it must be that the Braisa is talking about where he cannot save it later.
⑧ And even so, in the beginning it says, the finder can keep it, only if the owner already gave up hope.

lessons.chapter: The flood: beams, wood and stones
lessons.text: This lesson is his explanation of the step. The Hebrew words and his translation are in the previous lesson’s word sheet.
lessons.expl:
ΣSummaryWestwood · Feb 27, 2012 · 4:05
First part of the Braisa
Stated case
The finder may keep beams, wood, and stones that were flooded away since the owner already knew about it and willfully abandoned it.
Implied case
If the owner did not yet know of his loss and there was no prior willful abandonment, the finder may not keep it.
Ⅰ First explanation of Braisa
① The owner cannot save it later.
② If the owner would discover his loss later, he would surely give up hope.
③ Still, the Braisa says that prior knowledge by the owner and willful abandonment is required for the finder to keep it.
④ Without prior willful abandonment, the finder cannot keep it even though we know that the owner will surely give up hope when he finds out his loss.
⑤ Ⓐ A proof to Abaye.
Ⓑ Disproof to Rava.
Ⅱ Second explanation of the Braisa
① The owner can save it later.
② If he discovers his loss later, he would not give up hope.
③ Therefore, the finder can keep it only if there was prior knowledge of the owner and willful abandonment.
④ Without prior knowledge and willful abandonment, we cannot assume the owner will give up hope.
⑤ The Braisa is not talking about where the owner cannot save it later.
⑥ Perhaps the Braisa could hold that where the owner cannot save it later, even without prior knowledge and willful abandonment, the finder can keep it, since the owner will surely give up hope.
⑦ Therefore, the Braisa is not a proof against Rava.
Ⅲ Third explanation of the Braisa
① The owner can save it later on with great difficulty.
② If he discovers his loss later, he will not give up hope.
③ Therefore, in order for the finder to keep it, the owner must have prior knowledge and willful abandonment.
④ Without prior knowledge and willful abandonment, we cannot assume the owner will give up hope.
⑤ The Braisa is not talking about where the owner cannot save it at all later on.
⑥ In such a case, the Braisa would hold that even without prior knowledge and willful abandonment, the finder can keep it, since the owner will surely give up hope.
⑦ Therefore, the Braisa is not a proof against Rava.
End of the Braisa
① If the owner actively chases it, he does not give up hope.
② If he just stands passive, he does give up hope.
Ⅰ Cannot save it later on
The end of the Braisa makes sense.
Ⅱ Can save it later on
The end of the Braisa makes no sense, since chasing and standing do not indicate giving up hope.
Ⅲ Can save it later on with great difficulty
The end of the Braisa makes sense.
Ⓐ The end and beginning of the Braisa must be the same.
Ⓑ Therefore, the Braisa can be explained either like Ⅰ or Ⅲ, but not Ⅱ.
Ⓒ If like Ⅰ, it is a proof to Abaye / a disproof to Rava.
Ⓓ If like Ⅲ, no proof to Abaye / no disproof to Rava.

תָּא שְׁמַע כֵּיצַד אָמְרוּ הַתּוֹרֵם שֶׁלֹּא מִדַּעַת תְּרוּמָתוֹ תְּרוּמָה הֲרֵי שֶׁיָּרַד לְתוֹךְ שְׂדֵה חֲבֵירוֹ וְלִיקֵּט וְתָרַם שֶׁלֹּא בִּרְשׁוּת אִם חוֹשֵׁשׁ מִשּׁוּם גָּזֵל אֵין תְּרוּמָתוֹ תְּרוּמָה וְאִם לָאו תְּרוּמָתוֹ תְּרוּמָה וּמִנַּיִן הוּא יוֹדֵעַ אִם חוֹשֵׁשׁ מִשּׁוּם גָּזֵל וְאִם לָאו הֲרֵי שֶׁבָּא בַּעַל הַבַּיִת וּמְצָאוֹ וְאָמַר לוֹ כְּלָךְ אֵצֶל יָפוֹת אִם נִמְצְאוּ יָפוֹת מֵהֶן תְּרוּמָתוֹ תְּרוּמָה וְאִם לָאו אֵין תְּרוּמָתוֹ תְּרוּמָה לִיקְּטוּ הַבְּעָלִים וְהוֹסִיפוּ עֲלֵיהֶן בֵּין כָּךְ וּבֵין כָּךְ תְּרוּמָתוֹ תְּרוּמָה וְכִי נִמְצְאוּ יָפוֹת מֵהֶן תְּרוּמָתוֹ תְּרוּמָה אַמַּאי בְּעִידָּנָא דִּתְרַם הָא לָא הֲוָה יָדַע

His EnglishCome here! How is it… They said: The one that separates truma… that not from knowledge… his truma is truma? Behold! That he went down to inside the field of his friend… and he gathered… and he separated truma… that not with permission… if he is concerned because of thievery… not his truma is truma… and if not… his truma is truma… And from where does he know if he is concerned because of thievery? And if not? Behold! That he came… the owner of the house… and he found him… and he said to him: You should have gone by the better ones! If they are found… better ones… from them… his truma is truma… and if not… not his truma is truma… They gathered… the owners… and they added on them… whether like this… and whether like this… his truma is truma…….. And if they are found… better ones from them… his truma is truma? Why? At the time that he separated truma… behold! Not did he know!?

Gemara, Daf Chof Beis Amud Alef, ת״ש, line number 15
The Gemara now brings another Braisa to try and resolve the dispute between Abaye / Rava regarding the issue of whether potential giving up hope is enough, or you require prior actual giving up hope.
② How is it possible to separate terumah for someone else without prior permission from the owner, and still the terumah should be good terumah?
③ The Braisa continues:
Someone went into the field of his friend and separated terumah without prior consent from the owner.
④ If the owner, upon his discovery of it, considers it to be thievery, it is not good terumah.
⑤ If the owner does not consider it to be thievery, it is good terumah.
⑥ The Braisa continues by asking:
How are we to know whether the owner considers it to be thievery or not?
⑦ If the owner responds, you (the one who separated terumah) should have gone to the better ones.
Ⓐ If there are better ones.
The terumah is good terumah.
Ⓑ If there are not better ones.
The truma is not good truma.
The Braisa concludes by saying:
If the owner himself took produce and added it on to the produce that had been separated, then, for sure, the truma is good truma, even if he has no better ones.
⑨ The Gemara says: even in a situation where the owner had better ones, why should it be that the Truma that was separated, without his permission, should be good Truma?
⑩ Since the owner had no prior knowledge of this separation, even if we see clearly his mindset is to be pleased with the separation, even so, we need the mindset to be there from before.
So we see from this Braisa, that as long as we have a clear indication, later on, to indicate what his mindset would have been from before, we can look at it as if we already had that mindset from before.
This supports the opinion of Rava, who holds that definite potential giving up hope is considered to be as if the person already gave up hope from before.
Therefore, this Braisa is a proof for Rava and a dis-proof for Abaye.

·StatementWestwood · Mar 28, 2012 · 14:45
Gemara, daf chof beis. ה"נ, 18 lines from the bottom
① The Gemara now brings a proof to its explanation that our Braisa is talking about where the owner of the field had previously appointed his friend as his agent to separate terumah.
② The Gemara brings that the way in which we know that someone can appoint an agent to separate terumah is from the wording of the Pasuk which says:
"also you" …
③ from the extra word: "also" we learn out that you can separate terumah through an agent
④ since the appointing of an agent is learned out from the words the word also we compare the separating of terumah through an agent to the separating of terumah by the owner.
⑤ Just like when the owner separates his own terumah, it is with his knowledge, so too the separating of terumah through an agent must be with the knowledge of the owner.
⑥ So we see that without prior appointment as an agent, the other person cannot separate terumah.
⑦ The Gemara continues by going back and explaining the Braisa, which says that the friend separated terumah without the knowledge of the owner.
⑧ The Gemara explains that really the owner had already appointed his friend as his agent.
⑨ However, the normal way of the owner is to separate terumah from the middle quality produce.
⑩ The friend went ahead, without the knowledge of the owner, and separated terumah from better than average produce.
⑪ The Braisa is teaching us guidelines to determine when this act can be considered to have been included in his agency, and when not.
⑫ If the owner says: you should have gone to the better ones, and he has better ones, this reveals that better than average was included in his agency.
⑬ If he does not have better ones, this reveals that what was separated was not included in his agency and the terumah is not good terumah.
⑭ since the Braisa is not talking about reading the mindset of the owner based on what he reveals later on, to work retroactively, but only to be discussing what is or is not included in his prior agency. Therefore, this Braisa has no bearing on the dispute between Abaye and Rava.

Gemara, daf chof beis daled, אמימר, nine lines from the bottom
① Ameimar, and Mar Zutra, and Rav Ashi happened to be in the orchard of Mari bar Isak.
② The sharecropper of Mari gave them dates and pomegranates.
③ Ameimar and Rav Ashi ate them.
④ Mar Zutra did not.
⑤ Afterwards, Mari came and saw them eating.
⑥ He said to the sharecropper. Why didn't you give them from these better ones?
⑦ Mar Zutra still refused to eat.
⑧ Ameimar and Rav Ashi said to him: Why don't you eat? But we learned in a Braisa that says: If, by terumah, the owner says to his friend who had separated terumah for him from better than average produce: Why didn't you separate from the better ones? And he has better ones, the terumah is good terumah.
⑨ Mar Zutra answered, with a teaching of Rava: this response of: you should have gone to the better ones, and he has better ones, is only an indication of being pleased by terumah, since separating terumah is a mitzvah.
⑩ but in this case of the sharecropper, perhaps this response was made out of being ashamed to say differently … but not because the person is really pleased.
⑪ Therefore, Mar Zutra refused to eat.

lessons.expl:
12QuestionWestwood · Apr 30, 2012 · 10:58
Gemara, daf chaf beis, [?], ta shma, two lines from the bottom
① The Gemara now brings yet another source to try and resolve the issue disputed over by Abaye/Rava regarding whether actual giving up hope is required (Abaye) or potential giving up hope is good enough (Rava).
② The Gemara now brings a Braisa which discusses the rule stipulated by the Torah that produce, once it has become disattached from the ground, becomes vulnerable to becoming impure only if the produce had become wet after it was disattached
③ the Braisa says:
Ⓐ if dew fell on someone's produce and the owner discovered the produce while the dew was still on it, and he is pleased, the produce now qualifies to be vulnerable to becoming impure when coming in contact with a source of impurity.
This requirement of not becoming vulnerable to impurity unless it first came into contact with liquid, is contained in the verse in the Torah that says:
"when it shall be put" …
Ⓑ The Braisa concludes by saying: if dew had fallen on someone's produce and its owner discovered it after the produce had already dried, even if the owner was pleased with the fact that his produce had been wet with dew, the produce does not qualify to be under the rule of the pasuk that says:
"when it will be put" (when it will be put or when it shall be put, either one), which outlines the prerequisite that detached produce can become impure when coming into contact with a source of impurity only if the produce had previously become wet.
④ The Gemara now explains the apparent reason behind the distinction given by the Braisa that the produce becomes vulnerable to impurity only if the produce was discovered to be wet with dew while the dew was still on the produce but not if the discovery of the dew came after the dew already dried
⑤ the Gemara suggests that the explanation must be that even if the owner discovers the wetting of his produce with dew after it dried and he expresses such satisfaction that it is apparent that he would have surely reacted the same way had he discovered the liquid on his produce while it was still wet, even so the only way that the produce becomes vulnerable to becoming impure through contact with a source of impurity is if he saw the dew while it was still on the produce.
⑥ The reason must be because we do not say that a clear mindset after the fact can create the mindset from before
⑦ Therefore, this Braisa seems to be a support to Abaye and a disproof for Rava
